note: The reference here is the 1853 editor's, in his brackets, and his contraction is ambiguous. He writes `[*Ez.* ix. 6.]`, which in this volume could stand for either Ezekiel or Ezra — the two are elsewhere kept apart as `*Ezech.*` and `*Ezr.*` The verse is Ezra's: *I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God*, which is a countenance cast down and a confusion, exactly the posture and the affection the line names; Ezekiel ix. 6 is the order to slay at the sanctuary and has nothing to do with either. The volume settles it from inside itself — printed 171 prints the same verse in full as `*Ezr.* ix. 6, 7`, in the same penitential sense. Brightman reaches the same reading independently, tagging the sentence *Of Ezra*.

A promise about what God has done, asked back as a petition for what He has not yet done. Isaiah's verse is spoken by God in the perfect — *Delevi ut nubem iniquitates tuas, et quasi nebulam peccata tua*, I have blotted out thy transgressions — and the prayer answers *Dele … et dissipa*, blot thou out, scatter, with the possessive turned from *thy* to *mine*. The tense and the person are both reversed, and nothing on the page marks the change. It is the same move as at printed 321, where *let it not return unto me void* — said by God of the word that goes out of His own mouth — is asked of the prayer going up from a man's; twice in the volume a guarantee is borrowed rather than argued from.

This is the verse Part III mis-numbers, and here the volume gets it right. *Anni mei in luctu* stands at printed 409 under `Psal. xl. 9`, where the note has to say the reference is wrong; here the same half-verse is referred correctly to `Ps. lxxviii. 33`. So the edition proves its own misprint across three hundred and eighty pages — and it confirms, from inside the book, a reading that was otherwise established only from Brightman. Both kept as printed.

Psalm cxliii does not stop here — it runs on across the next two openings, the plate marking *Vers.* 9 and 10 below and *Vers.* 11 on printed 27. One psalm carries the morning prayer over three leaves, and a reader who meets only the tagged verse 8 will take it for a single borrowed line.

The same half-verse is cited twice in this book under two different numbers. At printed 34 it is *Substantia mea apud te est*, referred to `Psal. xxxix. 7`; here it is the same clause referred to `[Psal. xxxix. 8]`. The difference is the numbering, not the text: xxxix. 7 is the Authorised Version's figure and xxxix. 8 the Prayer Book's, which runs one ahead here. And the Prayer Book's figure is the one in square brackets — the 1853 editor's own mark for a reference he supplied. So the plate cites Andrewes' psalm on the AV's numbering and the editor cites it on the BCP's, on two pages of one book. Both stand as printed.

The plate cites `Psal. xliii. 1`, and the verse is Psalm lxiii. 1. *Ad te de luce vigilo* is the Vulgate of Ps. lxii. 2, the AV's *early will I seek thee*; Ps. xliii. 1 is *judge me, O God, and plead my cause*, which is not this line. The likeliest mechanism is a dropped letter — `xliii` for `lxiii` — the same slip the volume makes at printed 411, where `lxviii` stands for `lxxviii`. Kept as printed.

Under these seven Greek words for sin the manuscript sets a Hebrew column, and the 1853 left it out. The apograph gives `יצר` · `שגגה` · `אשם` · `חטאה` · `פשע` · `עון` · `תועבה` — *yetzer, shegagah, asham, ḥaṭṭa'ah, pesha, avon, to'evah*, the standard rabbinic vocabulary of sin, set as a lexicon beneath the Greek. It is not in the printed book at all. And the first of them is the word Andrewes glosses `יצר טוב`, the good inclination, at printed 76: so his *φαντασία* is being read through the rabbinic doctrine of the two inclinations, which is a fact about his theology and not a footnote about his text. Recorded here; not restored to the page.

The same psalm, correctly numbered here. At printed 92 *Ad te de luce vigilo* was referred to `Psal. xliii. 1`; here `Psal. lxiii. 7, 8` stands right. The volume therefore knows the psalm's number and mis-set it fourteen leaves earlier — which is the argument for calling that one a compositor's slip rather than Andrewes' own reckoning.

The plate cites `Rom. v. 2`, and the verse is Rom. v. 20. *Superabundavit gratia* is the Vulgate of Romans v. 20 word for word; v. 2 is *access by faith into this grace*, a different sentence. And the volume proves it against itself: printed 103 cites `Rom. v. 20` correctly. A dropped nought, kept as printed — the fifth place in this edition where one page corrects another.

The Creed again, but each article answered by what it did. Not *he was crucified* but the cross taking away the curse of the law; not *he rose* but the firstfruits; not *he sitteth* but the appearing and interceding. Compare printed 48, where the same articles are answered by a discipline the believer owes each of them. The Creed is recited three times in Part I and never twice to the same end.

From here to the foot of the next leaf the page is Daniel's prayer, ix. 5–19, quoted straight through, and the plate marks every verse of it — `[*Vers.* 7.]` `8.` `16.` `17.` `18.` `19.` They are not tagged one by one because the English lines are the verses; what the reader needs is to know he has entered a single prayer and not a catena. It is the great penitential prayer of the exile, made while Daniel was reading Jeremiah and counting the seventy years. And the volume comes back to it in Part II out of order — `ix. 19` closes §22 at printed 339 and `ix. 16` opens the intercession at printed 343, the later verse first. Part I prints the prayer whole and in sequence; Part II quarries it. Neither is conformed to the other.

Lines 6–15 run 1 John i. 8 to ii. 2 continuously — the confession, the promise to the confessing, the Advocate, the propitiation — and the plate marks the verses as it goes. But the last clause is not quoted, it is ASKED. John writes that Christ is the propitiation for our sins, *and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world*; the page turns the indicative into a petition — *let him be* the propitiation for my sins, *who is also for the whole world*. The world keeps the indicative and the man asks for himself. It is the method of printed 22 and 332 working inside a single sentence of Scripture.

`Psal. xxvii. 15` is not an error: it is the Prayer Book's numbering. The Authorised Version has this verse at xxvii. 13; the BCP Psalter, which divides the psalm differently, has it at 15 — and the BCP is the book Andrewes had to hand, as printed 433 shows twice over. Do not "correct" it. The volume moves between the two numberings without warning, and only reading the verse tells you which is in use.

The Passion assembled out of six books, and half of it proved from texts that are not narrating it. The thorns, the revilings, the strong cry, the neck under the cross and the pierced heart come from Matthew and John, who were telling the story; but the plowed back is the Psalter's *the plowers plowed upon my back*, the pierced hands and feet are Psalm xxii, the covered sin is Psalm lxxxv, the strong crying and tears are an epistle's account of Christ's prayers, and the broken body an epistle about a supper. Half the members of the catalogue are proved from outside the Passion narratives, which is why the sequence reads as prayer and not as recital — the same method as printed 313, where the nailing is proved from after the resurrection, out of Thomas's mouth.

The psalm says *turn US* and the plate says *turn ME* — and changes nothing else in the line. Ps. lxxxv. 4 is *Converte nos, Deus salutaris noster, et averte iram tuam a nobis*; the page sets *Converte me, Deus salutaris noster, et averte iram tuam a nobis.* One pronoun is made singular and the two around it are left plural, so he puts himself alone under the verb of turning and leaves the congregation in possession of the mercy. Lines 1–10 are Ps. lxxxv. 3–7 quoted whole, every verse marked by the plate, so the verses are not tagged one by one. Third instance of the pronoun pattern — with printed 342's *adauge mihi fidem* for the apostles' *nobis*, and 343's *in diebus nostris* for Hezekiah's *meis* — and the only one where the change is partial inside a single line.

`Psal. xlii. 10` is the Prayer Book's figure, not a slip. The Authorised Version has *my prayer unto the God of my life* at xlii. 8; the BCP Psalter numbers it 10. The same verse is cited the same way at printed 433, four hundred pages later — so the book is consistent in this, and it is further evidence that the Prayer Book Psalter was physically to hand. Do not correct it.

The psalm the volume mis-numbered at printed 92 stands here correctly as `lxiii. 1` — the third page to give it right, after 106. The book's own consistency is what convicts the one page that differs.

The page is a legal brief made of precedents, and every one of them is a place Christ was received by the unfit. A cave and a manger, a leper's house, a sinful woman, her mouth, a thief on a cross — five occasions, five citations, and the conclusion drawn from them is *Digneris ipse et me*, vouchsafe me also. He is not asking for an exception; he is arguing from a settled practice. It is the same method as §23's catena four hundred pages later, and the same as the ladder of unworthiness at printed 338, which is likewise built entirely out of approaches that succeeded.

The same clause, two verse-numbers, three hundred pages apart. *Memorare quæ mea substantia* is referred here to `Psal. lxxxix. 47` and at printed 35 to `lxxxix. 46`. The Authorised Version has it at 47, so the earlier page is the one that slipped. Both kept as printed — this is the seventh place where the volume settles one of its own references by citing it correctly elsewhere.

`Rom. v. 20` again, and cited right. This is the third page to give the verse correctly — with printed 103 and 111's own facing evidence — against the `Rom. v. 2` at printed 111. And note what he does with it: the Vulgate's indicative *superabundavit gratia*, grace did abound, becomes the subjunctive *superabundet*, let it abound. He turns a statement of what happened into a request that it happen again.

Four names for four ways a people is lost, and none of them is explained. Asshur is the foreign power a nation is given over to; Jeroboam the ruler who divides worship to keep a throne; Rehoboam the ruler who answers roughly and loses ten tribes; the evil spirit of Shechem the discord God sends between a man and his own city. As at printed 204, the deprecation depends entirely on the reader knowing the histories, and the English can only name them.

The plate's *cxxvii. 3* is not a slip. On the Prayer Book's numbering *he giveth his beloved sleep* is verse 3; the Authorised Version makes it verse 2. With the two Prayer Book references at printed 433 this is a further sign of which Psalter lay open. And Andrewes does not ask simply for sleep: *somnum sanitatis*, the sleep of soundness — the health that sleep is the evidence of, rather than the sleep itself. Neither English Bible has the word, and our English keeps it.

The verse the Latin question turned on returns here, and reads differently. At printed 34 the Latin renders this same *Ps.* cxxxviii. 8 as *Figmenta* manuum tuarum — a word that answers neither the printed Greek (τὰ ἔργα) nor the Vulgate (*opera manuum tuarum*), and can only come from a Greek text reading πλάσμα, which is what the Wright apograph reads. It is the strongest single evidence that the 1853's Latin is not merely construed from its own Greek. Here in Part II the same verse is plain *Opus* manuum Tuarum. The two are not in conflict — Part I sets a Latin against a Greek and Part II has no Greek to answer — but the contrast is worth a reader's eye, and it belongs to the introduction's case rather than to a correction of either page.

A reproach turned into a plea, and answered in the same line. The disciples' *carest thou not that we perish?* is spoken in fear and something like accusation; Andrewes takes the question over as a ground of pleading and then answers it himself — *Imo pertinet*, nay, Thou carest. He does the same with the storm at printed 286, where the verse serves the hour of prayer rather than the plea. The *Preces* uses a text more than once and never for the same thing twice.

The same Vulgate line as printed 34, doing different work. There *Memorare quæ mea substantia* was stacked against *Substantia mea apud te est* four lines above it, and the whole join depended on the shared *substantia* — a pun the Authorised Version dissolves, rendering one *my hope is in thee* and the other *remember how short my time is*. Here the verse stands alone, pleading the weakness of nature, and there is no join to protect; so the English can be plain where at 34 it had to keep the word.

The volume proves another of its own misprints, and this is the fourth time. Here `*Psal.* cxxx. 3` is cited correctly for *if thou shouldest mark iniquities*; at printed 40 the same verse is cited `*Psal.* cxxx. 30`, in a psalm that has eight verses. Both stand as printed. The pattern is now well established — printed 25 confirming the reading at 409, §17 confirming `Job. xiv. 4` against Part III's `xiv. 14`, §37 confirming `Is. xxxviii. 15` — and it is worth more than any conjecture, because the corroborating witness is the book itself.

The same numeral means two different psalms in this volume, and this page proves it. Here `*Psal.* cxvii. 2` is right on the Authorised Version's numbering — Ps. cxvii has two verses and this is the second. At printed 274 the plate cites `*Ps.* cxvii. 25` for the Hosanna, which is impossible on that numbering and can only be the Vulgate's cxvii, our cxviii. Neither is an error; the 1853 simply does not hold to one Psalter's numbers, which is why every note in this edition that touches a psalm number says which system it means, and why the plate's own figure is never altered.

Six parables chosen on one principle. The two debtors, the man half-dead, the Publican, the servant owing ten thousand talents, the lost sheep, the eleventh-hour labourer — every one turns on somebody who cannot pay, cannot walk, cannot plead, or came too late. The brace is not a survey of the parables but an argument assembled out of them, and it is the same argument the *Allegatio* made at printed 288 from the eleventh hour.

The Sayings are all one saying, and they are stacked so the negative turns into the positive. *Not* to condemn the world — *not* to judge it — *not* to call the righteous — *not* to destroy men's lives: four refusals in a row, each followed by what He came for instead, until *the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost* arrives without a negative at all and the series can end on the ransom. Andrewes prints no comment and needs none; the order does the work. A later pass that tidies the repetitions of *veni non… sed* destroys the figure, exactly as tidying the divided Psalm xci at printed 431/433 would.

The second half of the list is the same material as printed 307, doing the opposite work. Those who gainsaid Him, would cast Him down headlong, twice took up stones, blasphemed, preferred Barabbas — every one of these stood two pages back among the mercies *given thanks for*. Here they are entered as examples, that is, as instances of what He bore, and the catalogue runs on into the death itself. The *Preces* uses its material more than once and never for the same thing twice, and the two passages must not be conformed or cross-referred in the text: the repetition is the design.

This catalogue also stands in PART I at printed 154, in the same Latin words — *Caput spinis coronatum · Oculi lacrymis perfusi · Aures conviciis oppletæ · Os felle et aceto potum · Cor lancea perforatum* — phrase for phrase, same order, same proof-texts. What differs is the grammar, and with it the frame: Part I sets the list ACCUSATIVE under a brace cued *Per*, one long phrase *pleading* the Passion; here it is NOMINATIVE and numbered, an inventory of what was suffered. This is a Part I / Part II recension parallel, the first recorded — the known ones run between Parts II and III. Neither may be conformed: Part II splits *Manus et pedes perfossos* in two and adds the knees and the breast; Part I keeps the bloody sweat at the head and Part II drops it. The divergences are the evidence.

A second column of one word each, naming what the suffering was. Against *to be stripped naked* stands Shame, against *to be stretched on the cross* stands Pain — the same device as the *Dolor · Pudor · Maledictum* of printed 310, and as the orders-and-gifts columns at 304. The 1853 sets these hard right and they are not glosses on the Latin but a separate register running down the page, so they must survive into both layers; dropped, the catalogue loses the only place where it says what it is doing.

The nails are evidenced from AFTER the resurrection, and that is the method of the whole catalogue. No Gospel narrates the act of nailing; so for *clavis configi* Andrewes cites John xx. 25 — the print of the nails, as Thomas demanded to see it eight days later — and for the hands and feet dug through he cites a psalm. The same thing was noted at printed 154, where the Passion is assembled out of five books and not one of them a Gospel account of it. He is not narrating the Passion; he is proving it, and a text that shows the scar serves better than one that would only describe the blow.

The run closing here, printed 310–314, is a FOUR-GOSPEL HARMONY and the plate marks nearly every verse — which is why those leaves could not be tagged one by one; 312 alone carries twenty-five references. The four narratives are walked forward in step — Matthew xxvi into xxvii, John xviii into xix, Luke xxii into xxiii, Mark xiv into xv. He is not following one evangelist and supplementing him; he is reading all four abreast.

The wounds are then made to forgive, member for member. The glorious head wounded forgives what was offended *by the senses of the head*; the hands dug through forgive unlawful touch and unlawful working; the side pierced forgives the thoughts of the heart; the feet fastened forgive *the going of feet swift to evil*. The Passion catalogue has become a confession keyed to the same anatomy, part answering part — the fuller form of the device that broke out for four lines at printed 311, where the silence before the judge answered the mouth and the cords answered the hands.

A plea offered by proxy: he asks Christ to present the Passion to the Father on his behalf. Seven items are named — the death, the opened side, the blood and water, the begging of the body, the taking down, the burial in another's tomb, the three days — and then, rather than pleading them himself, *obsecro ut digneris hæc omnia pro me Patri Tuo offerre*. This is the *Allegatio*'s method (printed 291–299) handed over: the grounds are the same, but the advocate is now asked to make the argument. And what is added at the end is not an event but a motive — *the bitternesses which Thou didst suffer, the Love above all wherewith Thou didst suffer.*

The Spirit's history is given an Old Testament first, and it begins at the second verse of Genesis. Before the visible coming, the brooding upon the waters — *the sending-forth* follows, and the whole Old Testament work is catalogued as its own brace before the New begins. And a third register appears in the left margin from here: single words — Shadow, and its fellows below — naming the *mode* of each coming, as *Shame* and *Pain* named the members' sufferings at printed 313. They are the plate's, they are structural, and they must not be read as part of the line they stand against.

The *Triumph of Mercy* is the *Allegatio* again, with the grounds narrowed to one attribute. The same forensic shape as printed 291–299 — numbered heads, each a reason the plea must succeed — except that every head is now some aspect of mercy itself: the Name and its glory, the promised truth and the oath interposed, the consolation of love, the bowels of mercies, and then mercy great, manifold, of old, plenteous, its riches and its overflow. The numbering runs continuously across the braces, 1 to 13, so a brace here is a grouping inside one series and not a series of its own; a later pass that renumbers within a brace breaks the count.

Paul's four dimensions measure mercy here, and measured the WOUND at printed 315. *Μῆκος, Πλάτος, Βάθος* — length, breadth, depth — are Eph. iii. 18's measure of the love of Christ, and Andrewes fills each from the Psalter: from everlasting to everlasting for the length, up to heaven and down to hell for the depth, *upon all* for the breadth. Four pages earlier the same figure was turned on the man praying — *behold the multitude, the length, the breadth, the depth of them, from the head even to the heel* — to measure his hurt. The same Pauline measure serves the injury and the mercy, and the two passages must not be conformed or cross-referred in the text. It is the fourth time in this Part that a text is used twice and never for the same thing.

A second case of one verse cited by two different numbers in the two Parts. *I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner* is `*Psal.* xxxix. 12` here and `*Psal.* xxxix. 14` at printed 261. Twelve is the Authorised Version's figure exactly; fourteen answers to no system cleanly, the Prayer Book making it thirteen, so Part I's may be a slip of one rather than another Psalter. The pairing is what matters, and it is the same phenomenon as the pierced hands and feet at printed 154 and 312, cited xxii. 17 and xxii. 16 — there unambiguously Prayer Book against Authorised Version. Two independent instances now show the two Parts numbering the same psalm differently, which is why no figure in this edition is ever reconciled to another.

This is the reference the volume elsewhere gets wrong, and here it is right. `*Job* xiv. 4` — *who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?* — stands correctly on this page; at printed 406, where Part III makes its own confession out of the same material, the plate prints `*Job.* xiv. 14`, which is *if a man die, shall he live again?* Both stand as printed and neither is mended. The corroborating witness is the book itself, which is worth more than any conjecture, and it is now the fourth such case — with `Is. xxxiii. 15` against §37's `xxxviii. 15`, `Psal. cxxx. 30` against printed 297's `cxxx. 3`, and printed 25 confirming the reading at 409.

The confession is made entirely in other men's words. Eleven numbered admissions follow, and not one is Andrewes' own sentence: *I have sinned, I have done unjustly* is the Psalter's, *I have dealt wickedly in the covenant* is Solomon putting words into the mouth of a people not yet carried away, *I have grieved the Spirit* is Isaiah's account of the wilderness generation, *I have gone after my own thoughts* is Jeremiah quoting the people's defiance. Each is a third-person or plural indictment turned into the first person singular — the accusation accepted rather than answered. It is the same method as the Passion catalogue at printed 313: he is not describing his case, he is proving it, and the proof-texts are the confession.

Almost every text here states in the indicative what God HAS done, and is asked back as an imperative. Nathan told David *the LORD hath put away thy sin*, and the page prays *Transfer*; Hezekiah sang *thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back*, and it prays *Dissipa*; the psalm says *thou hast covered all their sin*, and it prays *Tege*. The Baptist's is the clearest: *ὁ αἴρων*, the participle that names Christ, becomes the bare imperative αἶρε. And it is not a device of one page — printed 22 asks Isaiah's *I have blotted out thy transgressions* back as *blot thou out mine*, 321 asks of a man's prayer the promise made of God's own word. What twice looked like a liberty is the method, and it is nowhere argued for.

The same six Greek words have now done two different jobs on three consecutive leaves. At printed 326 Paul's marks of godly sorrow — *ἀγανάκτησις, φόβος, ἐπιπόθησις, ζῆλος, σπουδή, ἀπολογία* — were the affections repentance feels, listed under impersonal verbs. Here they are the resolutions it makes, and the verbs are first person singular and active: *I have sworn, I have longed, I desire, I am zealous, I am earnest, I plead.* Paul's list is not being repeated; it is being conjugated. The pass has now recorded five texts used twice and never for the same thing, and this is the largest of them — six words at once.

The volume proves its own method from inside itself, on one verse. Isaiah xliv. 22 stands at printed 22 as *Dele … et dissipa* — blot thou out MINE, an imperative in the man's mouth — and it stands here in the indicative and in God's, *I blot out, as a cloud, thine iniquities*, with *return unto me, and I will redeem thee* left attached. Same verse, both ways, in one book, and neither place notes the other. What printed 328 shows as a habit is confirmed here by the plainest possible witness: the edition never has to argue that the imperatives are turned indicatives, because the book turns one back.
Isa. xlii. 3 — *a bruised reed shall he not break*, the verse Matthew quotes at printed 329

The confession borrows the words of a man who was stoned for the sin he confessed. Achan's *I have sinned, and thus and thus have I done* is used here as the form of an honest confession, and it is, precisely: the one confession in Scripture that names the deed in detail. The page takes the formula and not the outcome. The valley of Achor, where that story ends, has already been prayed against twice in this volume, at printed 205 and 282; here the man who made it is spoken with rather than deprecated.

Here the turn from indicative to imperative is visible IN THE GREEK, and the plate does it in the open. Matthew writes *κάλαμον συντετριμμένον οὐ κατεάξει* — he shall not break the bruised reed, a statement about Christ. The plate prints *κάλαμον συντετριμμένον* μὴ κατεάξῃς — a prohibition addressed to Him. This verse has now stood on three consecutive leaves and never twice the same way: at printed 329 as *Extirpa*, at 332 as Isaiah's own promise in God's mouth, and here as a petition in the second person. Whatever else the notes record about this edition's method, it can be shown on one verse in three openings, and the third of them shows it in the original.

The clincher of a courtroom argument is a question asked in a boat. *Perimus* stands twice in three lines — *if thou admit it not, we perish*, then Mark's *doth it not concern thee, if we perish?* — so the appeal's own word is caught up and handed back by Scripture, and the section ends not on a plea but on the disciples' reproach. This verse has now been used four times in the volume and never once the same way — at printed 172 as one of the Gospel cries, at 286 and 294 for two different things again, and here as the last word of a legal appeal. Never conform or cross-refer them.

A rising ladder of words for mercy, and it is the second of its kind in Part II. *Multitudo · magna multitudo · divitiæ · abundantia · superabundantia* — five terms, each stronger than the last, each with its own proof-text, ending on Paul's compound. This is what printed 319 does in Greek with περισσεία · πλεονασμός · ὑπερπλεονασμός · ὑπερπερισσεία, a ladder built out of prefixes; here the same figure is built in Latin out of different words. The two must not be conformed or cross-referred in the text — but they are one habit, and the summit of both is *superabundare*, which is why the sentence that follows sets the man's abounding transgression against it.

The same six titles, in this order and in these mysteries, stand again at printed 402–403, in Part III's Harley recension, turned from thanksgiving into belief — and there they carry not one reference. This is the only page where the catena behind them is visible. The two lists are not conformed and must not be.

The apostles asked this together; he asks it alone. Luke xvii. 5 is *adauge nobis fidem*, prayed by the twelve at once; the plate sets *adauge mihi*. A prayer made in company is taken into a closet — as at 327 with Stephen's prayer for other men, and 335 with Paul's oath about his kinsmen, and never marked. The mustard seed on the next line is the Lord's answer, ver. 6.

Not a description of faith but a concordance of the word. Nine epithets, each with its reference, and every one is the adjective its own verse attaches to *fides*: dead, Jas. ii. 20; unfeigned, 2 Tim. i. 5, *fide non ficta*, which the plate reverses to *non hypocritica*; working by love, Gal. v. 6, *fides quæ per caritatem operatur*; working with works, Jas. ii. 22, *fides cooperabatur operibus*; ministering virtue, 2 Pet. i. 5; overcoming the world, 1 John v. 4, *hæc est victoria … fides nostra*; most holy, Jude 20, *sanctissimæ fidei vestræ*. He has collected every place the word is qualified, set the three that condemn against the five that commend, and made the definition out of the collection. Third leaf running built this way — the six titles at 340, the four cells at 341 — the method of the section, not a mannerism. Only *non temporariam* is not an epithet of faith in its text: Rev. ii. 13 praises Pergamos for holding fast in the days of Antipas, so the fault is named by its opposite.

Dan. ix. 16 — *let thine anger be turned away from thy city* — unmarked in the plate, but Daniel's at the exile, and the volume printed ix. 19 of the same prayer at 339. It takes up Daniel's intercession in reverse, the later verse first.

The scripture foot is empty here and on the next leaf, and that is correct: every line is a psalm quoted whole with its reference beside it, so a tag would set the verse under the verse. The figures are a hybrid, checkable twice on this page. *Ps.* lxxxix. 16 — the AV divides that psalm so the verse is 15; the Vulgate, calling the psalm 88, has 16. *Psal.* lvii. 12 — AV 11; Vulgate, calling it 56, has 12. The plate keeps the Vulgate's verse-figure under the Hebrew psalm-number, which is neither system entire — a fourth kind of numbering after the plain AV at 300, the plain Vulgate at 274 and the BCP at 433. An introduction claiming one Psalter is answerable for this page.

The catalogue is the Roman law of persons. *Liber* against *Verna* is not free against slave but free against a slave born in the house; *Legitimus* against *Spurius* is the law of lawful issue; *Homo civilis* against *Barbarus*, citizen against outsider. He goes through the divisions of the *status personarum* one by one, giving thanks for a legal condition as another man might for health. The same catalogue stands again at printed 428, in Part III §4's *Quod* brace — with the antitheses stripped out (*Vivo · Ratione præditus · Civilis · Liber · Ingenuus · Honesta stirpe*). Here every good is defined by what he might have been instead; there they are simply goods. *Ingenuus* is the very term answering this page's *non Verna*. Not to be conformed: the antitheses are the whole difference.

The gifts are divided as the schools divided them — *bona gratiae, naturae, fortunae* — and only the first is subdivided, into redemption and calling. The same three stand again at printed 429 as *Pro bonis { naturæ … }*, the fourth recension parallel. Not to be conformed.

Gen. xxxii. 10 — Jacob at the ford, before meeting Esau: *I am not worthy of the least of all thy mercies, and of all the truth which thou hast shewed unto thy servant.* The volume has used this verse once already, at printed 338, where it stood first in a ladder of four sayings of unworthiness that were every one of them answered. Here it opens a confession instead. Never conform or cross-refer the two places.

Set V says the whole prayer out of the WISDOM books, almost all of it Proverbs — where sets I and II used men speaking in a story, this one uses a book of sentences. And its fourth petition is at last the natural one. After Job's self-curse at 351 and *man shall not live by bread alone* at 352, set V reaches Agur's *feed me with food convenient for me* — the one place in Scripture where a man asks for exactly daily bread. Three leaves, three treatments, and the plain sense comes last.

Prov. xx. 9 — *who can say, I have made my heart clean?*; Ps. xli. 5 — the plate's figure, which is the Vulgate's verse-number under the Hebrew psalm-number: the AV and the Prayer Book have it at xli. 4, *heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee*. Second page to show that hybrid, after printed 344.

A new section opens with a key, the plainest statement in the volume of how Andrewes reads a miracle. Five pairs read across: the world is the sea, men the fishes, the Church the boat, the preacher the fisherman, the Word the net. The draught of fishes set out as a working diagram for a man about to preach, hung on Peter's *we have toiled all the night and taken nothing*. This table IS read across — unlike the `Divisio` at 347.

Isa. lxiv. 9 — *be not wroth very sore, O LORD, neither remember iniquity for ever: behold, see, we beseech thee, we are all thy people.* The volume has used this verse once already, at printed 109, in the confession — here it is the fifth petition. Never conform the two places.

The same verse is said twice on this leaf, once in each language — Ps. xxvi. 8 stands in Latin at the door, *Domine, dilexi decorem domus Tuæ*, and returns fourteen lines later in Greek, Κύριε, ἠγάπησα εὐπρέπειαν οἴκου σου. The English renders both identically, which is the rule for a separated doublet; it is not a gloss and neither line may be dropped. He does not merely cite the Greek Psalter — he prays in it, which joins the coal at 355, the anaphora and the Greek formula at 349, and the doxology at 350.

Ps. xxxii. 6 — the plate's figure. *I said, I will confess my sins unto the LORD* stands at verse 5 in the Authorised Version and at 6 in the Prayer Book Psalter, which is what the plate follows here — a third numbering system on show in this volume, beside the plain Vulgate and the hybrid at 344 and 353.

§31 is the volume's THIRD treatment of the Lord's Prayer, and the method is confession. §25 set it out plainly (printed 350) and §26 said it seven times over in other men's words (351–354); here each petition is stated, then admitted to have been failed, then asked. *Holy art thou … to be held holy by all men, and by some more than by others, and by me first of all above many* — and then: *Yet I have not so held it.* The petition becomes an indictment before it becomes a request. The three treatments are not to be conformed; this is the only one that turns the prayer against the man praying it.
Dan. ix. 8 — the plate's figure. The words are verse 7's: printed 35 sets the same pair at ix. 7, and printed 133 prints the two verses in order under their own `Vers.` marks. Kept as printed.

Ps. cxxx. 3 — *if thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?* The same two lines stand verbatim at printed 41 under a figure reading cxxx. 30 — the closest witness the volume has against that misprint.

The last petition descends out of theology into the man's own week and ends in the present tense. The evils are anatomised downward — flesh, Fiend, penal evils, the world to come, the world that now is — and then stop being categories: the malice of THIS sickness, *wherewith I wrestle*, and the business I am entangled in. Both are present indicatives about the man holding the book — the same seam as the *Divisio* at 347–348.

The *Interpellatio Eucharistica* is the most doctrinally loaded line in Part II, and it is seven verbs long: *Recolo, gratias ago, admoneo, recordor, commemoro, offero, vel peto ut offeras*. *Admoneo* points the memorial at GOD — I put thee in mind — which is the patristic understanding of the anamnesis and not the ordinary Western one. And *offero* is qualified in the same breath by *vel peto ut offeras*: the sacrifice is offered, and then in one word the offerer is left an open question. A whole controversy hangs on *vel*, and the English keeps it there and settles nothing. This leaf belongs with the anaphora at 349 in any account of what rite the book was written out of.

The left brace is Philippians ii turned into nouns and run BACKWARDS. *Ἐκκένωσις* and *ταπείνωσις* are the substantives of *ἐκένωσεν* and *ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν*, and after them come the enfleshing and *σύλληψις ἐν γαστρί*, the conception in the womb: from the self-emptying down to the womb, later cause to earlier — the order of descent, not of narrative. *Ἐκκένωσις* is rendered emptying-out, not "exinanition" — the κένωσις opened at printed 305.

The Son of man with nowhere to lay his head returns here doing the opposite of what it did at printed 238. There it was turned round to indict the man praying — *no fit place to lay it here either, in me*; here it is simply pleaded, one of Christ's own hardships beside hunger and thirst and watching. Not cross-referred and not to be conformed: this volume uses a text twice and never for the same thing.

This is the *Commendatio Animæ* — the deathbed prayer of the Western books — put into Greek. The Latin runs *Libera, Domine, animam ejus, sicut liberasti Noe de diluvio · Abraham de Ur Chaldæorum · Isaac de hostia · Job de passionibus · tres pueros de camino ignis ardentis*, and it is among the oldest prayers the Church has, said over the dying. Andrewes keeps the form and changes three things: he turns it into Greek; he carries the roll on into the New Testament — the disciples in the storm, Peter in Herod's prison, Paul three times over; and he changes the petition from *his soul* to us, *καὶ ἡμᾶς ῥῦσαι*, so that a prayer for one man dying becomes a prayer the living say daily. The form is a Latin-West debt and the language is Greek, which is this book's whole difficulty on one leaf: it stands with the Litany at 358 and the memory-verses at 360 on one side, and with the anaphora at 349 on the other.

This sentence stands three times in Part II, and no two dresses agree. §24 opens with it at 345, §34 here, §41 at 384: *Magis deceret* · *Deceret magis* · *magis deceret*, and *confidens* · *confisus* · *confido*. Three sections begin by arguing he has no right to praise, and then praise. One word is not dress: 345, 374 and 384 read *ingenita* — thine inborn goodness — where this leaf alone reads *ingenti*, exceeding. The English follows the plate, and neither reading is claimed. 384 carries the office versicle too: §34 and §41 are near-twins, and are not conformed.

Under the Creed's own first word, *Πιστεύω*, stand five sentences and not one of them is a credal article. They are five men's confessions, each labelled with whose it is — DAVID'S · PAUL'S · JOHN'S · PETER'S · NATHANAEL'S, and the plate prints each man's text under his name. With §32's Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις at 363 this is the second section running that puts something else where the Creed's propositions should be — there the bare events, here other men's sentences. The band is silent on these lines by rule — the plate names its own speakers (§3). The practice of captioning a text with whose it is, which this edition's tags follow, is the author's own; see his blessings at 425.

The songs are taken in the Apocalypse's own order, from iv to xix, and the whole penitential sequence of Part II ends at the marriage supper: *blessed are they which are called unto the supper of the Lamb*. A book that began in confession closes at a table — which is where §32's Eucharistic pleading at 363 was already looking.

This is the one borrowed prayer in Part II set out whole and under its author's name, with book, chapter and corollary given. The contrast is the point: at printed 362 the volume took Augustine's most famous sentence — *hic ure, hic seca* — without a word of attribution, as it takes almost everything else. Here it stops, names a man, and gives a reference. Who he was, and the edition Andrewes is likely to have used, are in the list of sources at the back.

What follows is a SCHEMA, not a prayer — an outline of the parts of penitence with the text warranting each, like the *Divisio* at 347. The band selects rather than tags every warrant: the lines are single words, and each prints its own reference. The English keeps the outline an outline and does not make sentences of it.

Two bad bargains, and both are exchanges of a table for a trough. *What, for leeks and for garlick, the Bread of Angels?* is Israel in the wilderness craving what it ate in Egypt, set against the manna; *What, for the husks of swine, my Father's table?* is the prodigal. *Panem Angelorum* is the phrase from printed 361, where the fourth petition asked for the Angels' bread instead of daily bread. There he asked for it; here he asks how he came to trade it away — the same words doing opposite work, which this volume does constantly and never marks. The two lines that follow turn other men's words on the speaker: *who hath bewitched me* is Paul's rebuke of the Galatians, and *then was it better with me than now* is Hosea's adulterous wife resolving to go back to her first husband. The prodigal, the Galatians and the wife all say *I will return*.

This sentence has stood before, at printed 366, and it is worth the comparison. There: *whom I, a sinner, am not worthy to call upon, nor yet to name, nor to think upon in my heart*; here the same three verbs are braced and reordered — *not worthy to name · nor to call upon · nor to think in my heart* — and the clause that answers them is the same in both, *but for thy inborn goodness*. And that settles a question raised at 366. The volume reads *ingenita*, inborn, at 345, here, and at 384; printed 366 alone reads *ingenti*, exceeding. Three witnesses to one. Still kept as printed, and still nothing claimed — but the odds are now on the page.

The volume's own earlier page is the key to this unmarked one. *Ariditas mea, ariditas mea! væ mihi!* is the shape of Isaiah's *my leanness, my leanness, woe unto me*, with the book's own noun set into it — and printed 335 is where that noun was fastened to that verse, in a brace reading *woe is me { for my dryness, [Is. xxiv. 16] / for my hardness of heart, / for the drought of my eyes, [Jer. ix. 1] }*. Two of the three come back on this leaf with no reference at all — the dryness here, the *fountain of tears* eight lines down. A concordance made from the plate's marks would join neither.

And the page does the arithmetic. Seventy times seven is left as a figure of speech everywhere else; here it is multiplied out — four hundred and ninety times over — and the mercy is trusted for the whole sum. A rhetorical number made a countable one, which is the same literalism that made the Lord's Prayer's *earth* his own body at 361.

Romans vii. 18 stands here word for word and unmarked — *velle mihi adjacet; perficere autem non invenio*, to will is present with me; but how to perform I find not. The same verb was already doing the work four leaves back at 375, where the grief *lieth by me*, *qui mihi adjacet*. Paul's word for the will that lies to hand seeds the whole movement, and the plate marks it in neither place.

Two water-miracles are asked upon one heart, and the leaf ends on the first of them. *Thou that turnest even the flint into standing water* is the psalm's rock struck in the wilderness — and twenty lines later, *that I be not all flint*. The miracle is requested on himself. Between them stands *Rorate, cœli, desuper*, the Advent introit, with its object changed: the heavens are not asked to rain down the Just One but to *water the drought of my desert*. *Ariditas*, the drought, is the word of 376 and the word printed 335 fastened to Isaiah — it threads three leaves and is marked on none of them.

His tears having failed, he asks for a share in Christ's. *Of the tears of thy Christ impart to me some, which in the days of his flesh he shed abundantly* — and then the ground: *Supersunt in illo mihi, quæ in me mihi desunt* — there is left over in him for me what in myself is lacking to me. That is a treasury-of-merits sentence in a Church of England bishop's private book, applied not to satisfaction but to tears. Rendered plainly and unsoftened, which is the edition's rule; expect it to be noticed, as the prayer for the departed at 359 will be.

He quotes the psalm, credits it to another man, and unsays it in the next line. The plate puts the attribution in the running text — *(sic Psaltes, Psal. cviii. 1.)* — so that *my heart is ready* is David's and *I fear that mine is not* is his own. It is the volume's habitual movement inverted: everywhere else an indicative of God's is prayed back as a command and claimed; here an indicative of man's is quoted and declined. The three verbs following are the four-verb frame's third setting — *metuo … cupio … doleo si minus* — after the empty frame at 367 and §37's filled one at 378.

§39 opens at the foot of the page, the second attributed borrowing in Part II — where at 362 the volume took Augustine's *hic ure, hic seca* with no credit at all. The doubt raised at transcription is settled: the passage reads so like Augustine that the tag looked composite, but Brightman, working independently from the sources, also gives Fulgentius of Ruspe. The counsel turns on a word English cannot hold — *orator* is the man who prays and the man who speaks, so *let him be an orator before he is a teacher* means let him be a pray-er first, and the clause before it puns again on *oratio*. English chooses praying: the argument is about prayer, only the joke is about oratory.

A Latin imperative governs a Greek infinitive, and the line is one sentence. *Perge igitur* ἀγωνίζεσθαι ἐν προσευχαῖς — go on therefore to strive in prayers. The Greek is Colossians' own, where it is a participle describing somebody else: Epaphras, *ἀγωνιζόμενος ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐν ταῖς προσευχαῖς*, always striving for you in prayers. A report of what one man did is turned into the reader's own command — the volume's habitual movement, taken here on a participle rather than an indicative, as it was on the Baptist's ὁ αἴρων at 334. He did not think of himself as changing tongue mid-line, and the English keeps the sentence whole.

The section ends in Hebrew because no Latin or English Psalter will say what it needs. לך דומיה תהלה — Psalm lxv. 2 in the Hebrew numbering — to thee silence is praise, with the 1853's own literal gloss set beside it, *tacet tibi laus vel Psalmus*. The Vulgate takes the same consonants from another root and gives *Te decet hymnus*, praise befitteth thee; the Prayer Book has *Thou, O God, art praised in Sion.* Either would destroy the entry, which exists to say that praise falls silent — so the Hebrew stands and the English follows it. It is unpointed in the plate, without vowel or accent, and is the second Hebrew in Part II, after the Hosanna at 274.

Twice on this leaf the facing Latin is the only guard against a plausible misreading of the Greek. *Μακάρεσσι δαίμοσι* would give demons to anyone without the Latin's *Beatisque Angelis* — in this Homeric register δαίμονες are the blessed spirits, and "demons" would be a serious and pious-looking error. The next line carries the graver case: the poem's most famous cry stands set as Πᾶς, Θεὸς ὢν, ἔθανες — *πᾶς* cannot be construed at all, and the Latin's *Qui, Deus immortalis, mortuus es?* gives the interrogative. Πῶς, *how*: a wrong sort, kept as printed. Unlike the Hebrew at 386 this leaf survives in a single photograph, so there is no second copy to confirm it from.

This is Part II's printed 380 over again in the Harley recension, and the divergences are the whole point. At 380 the plate credits the line in its own running text — *Domine, paratum est cor meum:* *(sic Psaltes, Psal. cviii. 1.)* — so *my heart is ready* is David's, and what follows is *metuo ne meum non sit*, I fear that mine is not. Here the attribution is gone, and so is the *meum*: there is no other man's heart in view, so the psalm's words are spoken in his own voice and simply doubted. And the consolation goes with it. Part II answered the fear with *cupio certe* — I do at least desire — where Part III has only *Utinam esset paratum. Hei mihi quod non est.* A wish and a lament, with the desire taken out. Neither recension is conformed to the other.

The Creed begins again here, and this is the second of three passes over it. *I believe, Lord; supply the defects of my faith* answers the opening *help Thou mine unbelief* at 399 — and what follows is no longer what each article is, but what each Person is owed: the Father loved, the Almighty revered, the Creator trusted with a soul, the Son thanked. The articles have not changed; the verbs have.

This leaf carries two wrong references, and the volume gives the right reading for both of them elsewhere. *My days are consumed in vanity, and my years in anguish of heart* stands here under Psal. xl. 9; the verse is Ps. lxxviii. 33, and printed 25 cites that same half-verse correctly. The second is at the foot of the page (see below). Both are kept as printed. The corroborating witness in each case is this book, three hundred and eighty pages apart, which is a stronger warrant than any conjecture and is why neither is mended.

The second twin of §37, and it differs from its Part II fellow twice over. The chapter figure reads Is. xxxiii. 15 — *he that walketh righteously*, which is the opposite of what the line wants. The verse is Hezekiah's, Isaiah xxxviii. 15, and printed 372–373 cites it rightly. And the sentence itself has changed. Both recensions turn the Vulgate's *cum ipse fecerit* — when He hath done it — into *fecerim*, when I have; but §37 stammers it, *fecerim, fecerim, fecerim*, three times and with no object, where here it is said once and given one: *cum ipse hæc fecerim*. Where Part II could not get past the word, Part III names the thing done. Neither recension is conformed to the other, and the triple stands as a triple there.

An appeal is lodged from God to God, and it is a formal legal act. *I appeal therefore, O Lord, from Thee unto Thee* — *from Thee the just, unto Thee the merciful · from the seat of justice, unto the throne of grace · from Thee the judge, unto Thee the Father in Christ.* The court appealed from and the court appealed to are the same court, and what makes the appeal lie is not a second judge but the Incarnation: it is *the Father in Christ* who receives it. The forensic habit runs through the whole book — the *Allegatio* of §7, the *Interpellatio* of §32, the Areopagus at 386 — but this is the boldest of them, and the English keeps the legal words as legal words.

The ground of that appeal is God's own stated will, cited back to Him. *Who wilt have all men to be saved* (1 Timothy ii. 4) and *who wilt have no man perish* (2 Peter iii. 9) are set as a pair — two declarations of what God wills, entered as evidence against His justice and in favour of His mercy. The line above them is the disciples' *carest thou not that we perish?*, printed under Marc. iv. 28; the verse is iv. 38, and the volume cites it rightly at printed 286 and again at 294. Kept as printed, the third such figure in two leaves.

Having appealed away from the judgement seat, he sets one up himself. *But I judge myself · I think upon it again · I pronounce the sentence · I take vengeance myself upon myself*. This is the other half of the appeal at 410: justice was asked to stand aside there, and here the man supplies it in his own person, so that nothing is asked to be waived, only moved. *If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged* was quoted at printed 386 as a counsel; here it is an act performed — the same verse twice over and never for the same thing. Note the plate cites it there as 1 Cor. xi. 31 and here as xi. 30; the volume gives its own right figure, and both stand as printed.

This line is a cento of three places in Job, and it passes through three different texts of them without a mark. *The infant of one day* is Job xiv. 4 **as the Septuagint reads it** — *not one, even if his life be but one day upon the earth* — which the Vulgate does not say at all, its verse asking only who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean. Andrewes uses the phrase in his own voice in a Pentecost sermon and names his authority there: *infans unius diei super terram*, `as the Seventy read it`. Augustine had given it in the same Latin, *nec infans cuius est unius diei vita super terram*. The middle clause is Vulgate verbatim and from another chapter — Job xxv. 5, *stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus*, with *ipsæ* added and *ejus* turned to *Tuo*. The last clause is Job iv. 18 and is not the Vulgate either: that reads *in angelis suis reperit pravitatem*, found depravity, where this has *respexisti insipientiam*, folly, which is the Hebrew's word and the Authorised Version's. Whether he took it from a Latin made out of the Hebrew or turned it himself is not settled. The plate's figure covers none of the three: Job xxv. 3 is *is there any number of his armies?* Kept as printed. Brightman's margin supplies the two outer references and none for the stars. And Job xiv. 4 is the verse this book cites rightly at printed 323 and misnumbers at 406 as xiv. 14 — quarried here a third time, with no page marking the other two.

The fourth property of mercy is *fellow-suffering*, and it is not softened. *Though we deserve it, yet He grieveth with us in our calamity* — and the name for it is Zacharias' *tender bowels of His mercy*, the *viscera misericordiæ*, which is an organ and not a sentiment. The close answers a concession made eight leaves back: at 411 the plea had granted that *God heareth not sinners* — John ix. 31, in the mouth of the man born blind. Here: *who not only heareth sinners, but also, in the day of their trouble, those who in the time of their peace despised Him.* The objection is not argued down; it is simply outlived.

Three men who would not take back a word, and the argument gains force as the witnesses lose worth. *If Isaac would not change his word* — the blessing got by fraud, *yea, and he shall be blessed* · *if the Persian would not, a heathen* — Darius, bound by the law of the Medes against his own friend · *if profane Pilate would not* — *what I have written I have written.* Then: *Surely God never will.* The series descends in dignity while ascending in strength, and ends on the man who condemned Christ. It is the same move as the appeal to Ahab at 412: the argument is strongest where the example is worst.

The plea is that one memory must not drive out another. Augustine: *Lord, look not so upon my sin that Thou shouldest therefore forget Thine own Name.* And the Name is not incidental to the argument — *Jesu, this is His name, because He saveth us from our sins*, so that to remember the Name is already to have granted the request. Shimei returns here from printed 412, where David sparing him was offered as a precedent; now it is the title that carries it — *Son of David*, who forgave Shimei … do Thou also forgive.

The verdict clause of the whole argument, and then the turn from proving to asking. *These things were not said in vain, they cannot be* — everything quoted since 415 has been entered as evidence, and this is the finding upon it. Three *wherefores* then mark the change of business: *wherefore … these Thy comforts have refreshed my soul* · *wherefore let us come boldly unto the throne of grace* · *now therefore hear, O Lord.* The case rested, the petition begins, and the throne appealed to is the one named at 410.

The thanksgiving begins before birth, and it is the exact counterpart of the confession at 406. Psalm cxxxix and Job x are laid together to make one embryology: *my substance in the lower parts of the earth* · *Thine eyes did see my imperfection* · *Thou hast milked me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese* · *clothed me with skin and flesh, and fenced me with bones and sinews.* Printed 406 began at the same place — *conceived in unclean seed, warmed in iniquity in my mother's womb* — and then went down the body member by member. The same body is catalogued twice in this Part, once as filth and once as workmanship, and neither page mentions the other.

Jacob is here for the third time in this volume, and each time it is a different clause of the same night. Here it is his prayer before meeting Esau — *I am not worthy of all Thy mercies … with my staff I passed over this Jordan, and now I return with two bands*, the whole of a life measured by what he set out with. At 422 it was *I will not let Thee go, except Thou bless me*; at printed 375 the wrestling was turned into a refusal — *give me another Thee; else will I not let Thee go.* One night at the ford, quarried three times and never for the same thing.

The book's last section returns to its first argument. *At evening, and morning, and at noonday will I pray* is the psalm the volume opened on at printed 2, where the canonical hours were built out of Scripture — a text found for each hour at which somebody in Scripture is praying — rather than inherited from a breviary. Four hundred pages later the hours are simply kept, without the argument, which is what it looks like when a case has been made and is being lived on.

Isaiah's promise is prayed back as a command for the third time in this volume, and here it is fitted to the hour. God says *I have blotted out thy transgressions as a cloud*; the prayer answers *Blot out, O Lord, as the cloud of night our iniquities, and as the morning mist our sins.* The cloud has become a night cloud and the mist a morning one — the figure adapted to the office it is being said at. The same verse stands at printed 22 already turned into a petition, and at printed 332 in God's own indicative, untouched. Three settings, and no page marks the other two.

One psalm is quarried across two leaves to cover the whole of a day. Psalm xci gives the night terrors on the leaf before — *the terror by night*, *the thing that walketh about in darkness* — and gives this leaf its daylight ones: *the arrow that flieth by day*, *the assault*, and *the noonday devil*. That last is the Vulgate against the Prayer Book, which reads *the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day*, and is one of the places where our English follows the Latin because Andrewes did; it was the same at printed 24. Morning, noon and night out of a single psalm.

The book ends on the pair it began with, and this time the reference is right. *Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth* and *let my speech be with grace, seasoned with salt* stood together in the same order at printed 26, near the volume's opening. There the plate cited the psalm as cxli. 8, where the words are verse 3; here it prints cxli. 3. The volume corrects itself across four hundred leaves, and both figures stand as printed.

Hezekiah's psalm returns for the evening office, and it is being thanked rather than prayed. *Who hast not cut off, like a weaver, our life, nor from the morning even unto the evening made an end of us* — the sick king's *I have cut off like a weaver my life*, turned from complaint into a benediction for the day survived. Isaiah xxxviii carried the whole of §37's confession and the twin at 409; here it does a third thing, and none of the three places refers to the others.

The Gospel's measure of forgiveness is taken over to count sins instead. *Seven times in the day the just man stumbleth* is Proverbs — *but we (miserable sinners) seventy times seven*. At printed 377 that figure was what God was required to forgive, and the page there multiplied it out to four hundred and ninety to make the demand exact. Here the same number counts the falls. The measure of mercy has become the measure of need, and neither page mentions the other.

The book ends on the sentence a man says going to sleep and says dying, and it has said it once before. *In peace, in the selfsame, will I sleep and take my rest* is the Compline psalm, *in idipsum*; and the last words of all are *Into Thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit, for Thou hast redeemed me*. That verse stood at printed 26, among the morning prayers, where the plate cited it on the Prayer Book's numbering. The volume opens its day and closes its life with one sentence, and the lamp two lines above has just made the two the same act. Nothing on either page marks the return.
